TO Margot
I think 'twill be A night of stars and snow,
My footsteps as I go; Nobody--nobody will be there
To see me in my bush of hair Dance burning through the night.
Upon this leafy bush
Flutters a thing of light, A twittering linnet.
Of dew and sun and air By this small parcel of life
As if each bramble-spray And mounded gold-wreathed furze,
Were only hers; As if this beauty and grace
And, at a flutter of wing, Might vanish in song.
Speak not--whisper not;
Softly on the evening hour, Secret herbs their spices shower,
Lean-stalked, purple lavender; Hides within her bosom, too,
Breathe not--trespass not;
Latticed from the moon's beams, Perchance a distant dreamer dreams;
The unseen ghosts of children fare, Faintly swinging, sway and sweep,
While, unmoved, to watch and ward, 'Mid its gloomed and daisied sward,
That one little leaden Lad.
'Thou solitary!' the Blackbird cried, 'I, from the happy Wren,
Perched all upon a sweetbrier bush, Have come at cold of midnight-tide
Grief smote thy heart so thou dost sing In solemn hush of evening,
Nay, nay, not sing, but rave, but wail, Most melancholic Nightingale?
All pinings of the day in sleep? Why, then, when rocked in starry nest
Doth thy lone heart delight to make Music for sorrow's sake?'
It seemed the whole world lay a-dream, Lulled by the watery sea.
Upon this stranger soft did look The Nightingale: sighed he:--
''Tis strange, my friend; the Kingfisher
Out of his green and gold to say Why thou, in splendour of the noon,
And else dost thee array In a most sombre suit of black? "Surely," he sighed, "some load of grief,
Must weigh upon his back!" Do, then, in turn, tell me, If joy
Why dost thou now, most Sable, shine In plumage woefuller far than mine?
Than any dirge I sing!'
Breathed a strange riddle both did share Yet neither could expound.
In the small knowledge of a man-- Have we an answer found?
Is hid even from themselves from sight; And some win peace who spend
Of finding consolation where Life has but one dark end;
A tale, as lovely as forlore, Into the midnight air.
The far moon maketh lovers wise
Lending curved cheeks, dark lips, dark eyes, A strangeness not their own.
In starless darkness peace to win, Even on that secret world from this
'I have no master,' said the Blind Boy,
Cowled in this hood, she sent me begging For whate'er in pity may befall.
'Hard was her visage, me adjuring,-- "Have no fond mercy on the kind!
Draw close ere striking--thou art blind."
'So stand I here, my woes entreating,
Point with her sparkling my barbed armoury, Shine on my silver-laced shoon.
'Oh, sir, unkind this Dame to me-ward;
In your sweet charity draw nearer The saddest rogue on Earth!'
You hunted me with all the pack,
By no wild hope of force or greed Could you make sure of me.
With tender breast aglow, The goddess in me laughed to hear
She laughed to think no mortal e'er
The very Cause that was the Hunt One moment could enmesh:
Stilled breath and vanquished eyes, He that hunts Love with horse and hound
'Step very softly, sweet Quiet-foot,
By this dark ivy stoop cheek and brow. Still even thy heart! What seest thou?'
'High-coifed, broad-browed, aged, suave yet grim,
Staring at nothing--that's me!--and yet, With a hate one could never, no, never forget...'
'This is my world, my garden, my home,
And bear me out of the dark into light, And happy I was in her tender sight.
'And then, thou frail flower, she died and went,
And that Old Woman--an Aunt--she said, Came hither, lodged, fattened, and made her bed.
'Oh yes, thou most blessed, from Monday to Sunday
Called me, "dear Nephew"; on each of those chairs Has gloated in righteousness, heard my prayers.
'Why didst thou dare the thorns of the grove,
Now thou hast peeped, and now dost know What kind of creature is thine for foe.
'Not that she'll tear out thy innocent eyes,
Watch thou, wait thou: soon will begin The guile of a voice: hark!...' 'Come in, Come in!'
Flee into some forgotten night and be
Beyond the rumour even of Paradise come, There, out of all remembrance, make our home:
Hollowed by Noah's mouse beneath the chair Wherein the Omnipotent, in slumber bound,
Perchance Leviathan of the deep sea Would lease a lost mermaiden's grot to me,
A music wistful for the sea-nymph's sake: Haply Elijah, o'er his spokes of fibre,
Spied, tranced in azure of inanest space, Some eyrie hostel, meet for human grace,
Lost in the uttermost of Eternity.
Might there not rest be found for wandering feet? Or, 'twixt the sleep and wake of a Helen's dream,
No, no. Nor earth, nor air, nor fire, nor deep
Somewhere there Nothing is; and there lost Man Shall win what changeless vague of peace he can.
The abode of the nightingale is bare,
The fox howls from his frozen lair: Alas, my loved one is gone,
It is winter.
The wild bee hung in the hyacinth bell, Light in effulgence of beauty fell:
I am alone: It is winter.
Starry Orion hunts o'erhead; Come moth, come shadow, the world is dead:
I am alone; It is winter.
See this house, how dark it is
Not one trembling leaflet cries To that Watcher in the skies-- 'Remove, remove thy searching gaze,
Brood not, Moon, so wildly bright, On secrets hidden from sight.'
'Secrets,' sighs the night-wind, 'Vacancy is all I find;
Wail a summons, faint and sad, No voice ever answers me,
'Once, once...' the cricket shrills, And far and near the quiet fills
Hush falls again.
Mark how the hours go. Every stone is mouldering slow.
Some minutest atom shake, Some fretting ruin make
Beneath these thick-boughed trees!
'Whom seek you here, sweet Mistress Fell?' 'One who loved me passing well.
Stranger, if in this lonely place Bide such an one, then, prythee, say
'Many his like, Mistress Fell?' 'I did not look, so cannot tell.
When his voice called me, I must go; Touched me his fingers, and my heart
'Why did he leave you, Mistress Fell?' 'Magic laid its dreary spell.--
Into his dream I tried to creep; Called his name, soft was my cry:
'The flower and the thorn are here;
Out of her bower the bird replies, Mocking the dark with ecstasies,
Praising what sleeps below!
'Thus have they told me. And I come,
Not tears I give; but all that he Clasped in his arms, sweet charity;
For a close whispering.'
'Who knocks?' 'I, who was beautiful,
I, from the roots of the dark thorn am hither, And knock on the door.'
'Who speaks?' 'I--once was my speech
When echo lurks by the waters to heed; 'Tis I speak thee fair.'
'Dark is the hour!' 'Ay, and cold.' 'Lone is my house.' 'Ah, but mine?' 'Sight, touch, lips, eyes yearned in vain.' 'Long dead these to thine...
Brake the flames of the stars. In gloom groped a hope-wearied hand
A face peered. All the grey night
Nought but vast Sorrow was there-- The sweet cheat gone.
In the woods as I did walk,
I did with a Stranger talk, And his name was Dream.
Shady-wide his bonnet's brim; His horse beneath a silvery oak
Softly his breast-brooch burned and shone;
One of his hands held mine, and one The fruit that makes men wise.
Flowers white as milk did gleam; Spread to Heaven the Assyrian Tree,
Dews were still betwixt us twain;
Yet--not a whisper comes again Of the words he said.
She will not die, they say,
And hie away.
Then will seem all reverie, How black to me!
And every hope a memory, All gladness dead.
My weakest hour, and whisper to me, And coldly go.
Clothed in its mortal beauty I shall see, And, waking, weep.
In man's false Heaven my peace to be: All blind, and blind.
Why did you flutter in vain hope, poor bird,
'Twas but a sweet, false echo that you heard, Caught only a feint of day.
Burn yet the unanswering stars. And silence brings The same sea's desolate surge--*sans* bound or mark--
Fret now no more; be still. Those steadfast eyes,
Only with beauty wake wild memories-- Sorrow for where you are, for where you would be.

O all ye fair ladies with your colours and your graces, And your eyes clear in flame of candle and hearth, To'rd the dark of this old window lift not up your smiling faces, Where a Shade stands forlorn from the cold of the earth.

God knows I could not rest for one I still was thinking of; Like a rose sheathed in beauty her spirit was to me; Now out of unforgottenness a bitter draught I'm drinking of, 'Tis sad of such beauty unremembered to be.
Men all are shades, O Women.--Winds wist not of the way they blow. Apart from your kindness, life's at best but a snare. Though a tongue now past praise this bitter thing doth say, I know

Strange, strange, are ye all--except in beauty shared with her-- Since I seek one I loved, yet was faithless to in death. Not life enough I heaped, so thus my heart must fare with her, Now wrapt in the gross clay, bereft of life's breath.
When music sounds, gone is the earth I know,
Her flowers in vision flame, her forest trees, Lift burdened branches, stilled with ecstasies.
Naiads whose beauty dims my waking eyes, Rapt in strange dream burns each enchanted face,
When music sounds, all that I was I am
While from Time's woods break into distant song The swift-winged hours, as I hasten along.
I was at peace until you came
I lived in quiet; cold, content; All longing in safe banishment,
Made wisdom unwise.
To seek a lodging. Quite forgot Lay the sweet solitude we two
Time's cold had closed my heart about; And shut you out.
Take all the little all I have! Strip me of what in voiceless thought
Reverie and dream that memory must Hide deep in dust!
The haunted house you have chosen to share, Still 'neath its walls the moonbeam goes
Still o'er its broken roof-tree rise The starry arches of the skies;
The thunder of an ebbing sea.
'Tis not my voice now speaks; but as a bird
Pleads on till distant echo too hath heard And doubles every note:
Would cry and waken thee.
All the night waits thee, yet thou still dream'st on. Furtive the shadows that about thee creep,
Unseal thine eyes, it is my heart that sings, And beats in vain its wings.
Lost in heaven's vague, the stars burn softly thro'
Within its lovely labyrinth, and know Mute seraphs guard the way
To that self's self it still is dreaming of.
I am that Adam who, with Snake for guest,
I am that Adam who, with broken wings, Fled from the Seraph's brazen trumpetings.
A world where sin--and beauty--whisper of Home.
Pure daybreak lighten again on Eden's tree? Loosed from remorse and hope and love's distress,
No more with wordless grief a loved one grieve, But to heaven's nothingness re-welcome Eve?
After the songless rose of evening,
In nodding cavalcade advancing Starred the deep hill:
In your quiet wonder took All that glamour, peace, and mystery
Beauty hid your naked body, Time dreamed in your bright hair,
Burned far and fair.
The last light fails--that shallow pool of day!
Arch their wild necks, lift their wild heads and neigh; Their drivers, gathering at the water-brink,
Utter their hollow speech, or gaze afar, Rapt in irradiant reverie, to where
Come the wood-nymphs to dance within the glooms,
Ashen with twilight the dark forest looms O'er the nocturnal beasts that prowl within
Resounding roar wild torrent, hungry throat; While in the dew-drowsed branches' ebon hush,
'O glory of beauty which the world makes fair!' Pant they their serenading on the air.
The lusty charioteers their stations take; Planet to planet do the sweet Loves fly,
Cities of men, in blindness hidden low, Fume their faint flames to that arched firmament,
The unearthly are abroad, and weary and spent, With rush extinguished, to their dreaming go.
The glory of beauty are in one enravished face.
The burning fire shakes in the night,
With far-flung arms enflamed with light, The trees are lost in dream.
Lost in far-wandering desire, Hath in the darkling deep above
O strange devices that alone divide
The very highway of earth's pomp and pride That lies between
Of where he longs to be, But which, bound hand and foot, he, close on night,
Hearken, O dear, now strikes the hour we die;
Have proved a dream the world's realities, Turned each from other's darkness with a sigh,
On any other journey, but of death.
How each of us must prove Love's infidel; Still out of ecstasy turn trembling back
Of leaden day by day, and hour by hour, and be Of all things lovely the cold mortuary.
Why in my heart, O Grief,
Dead is my well-content, And buried deep my pride.
To hand and side.
Shut are the day's clear flowers, Now have her birds left mute
Lone shall we be, we twain, In the night hours.
And dark hair loosed, shalt see Take the far stars for fruit
And in the yew's black Shall the moon be.
Nor heed if in wandering air Die a lost song of love
Still as well-water be The thoughts we share!
Tryst from chill sepulchres, Dreamless our gaze shall sleep,
Heart unto heart will speak, Without tears.
Joy's strange disguise-- Shall be the last to fade
Ere the first dart of daybreak Pierce the skies.
What needest thou?--a few brief hours of rest
A transient silence wherein truth could say Such was thy constant hope, and this thy way?--
A livelong tangle of perplexities!
Some steadfast refuge from a fickle heart; Still to be thou, and yet no thing of scorn,
O riddle of life that is An endless war 'twixt contrarieties.
Leave this vain questioning. Is not sweet the rose?
Hath not in miracle brave June returned? Burns not her beauty as of old it burned?
So far in thine own mind away from home!
Where sleepeth echo by earth's music made, Where all things transient to the changeless win,
Dark is the night,
Hours--days--years, Into grey ashes go;
But sombre is the glow.
And the print is small; Mocking the winds
Feeble the fire that lends Its light withal.
Let thy shadowy hair, Blot out the pages
Be ours the one last leaf By Fate left bare!
And then Life's book put by; Turn each to each
Ere the last flame is gone To warm us by.
Old and alone, sit we,
Lost to earth's 'Listen!' and 'See!' Thought's 'Wherefore?' and 'When?'
Of a past once lovely, but now Wasted and faded away,
Vast broods the silence of night,
Lifts on our faces her light, Whence all dreaming is gone.
In their sockets our eyes are still; Desire as cold as the dead;
And One, with a lanthorn, draws near,
'Where art thou?' he asks: 'I am here,' One by one we arise.
A friend from the touch of that foe: Heart cries unto heart, 'Thou art old!'
O thou who giving helm and sword,
And starry dark's all tender dews To blunt and stain:
Unharmed, yet stricken sore; A living shape 'mid whispering shades
No trophy in my hands I bring,
The neighings and the trumps and cries Were but a dream--a dream.
O, of thy mercy deep, A dream my all, the all I ask
Now each man's mind all Europe is:
Daze every heart: O grave and wise, Abide in hope the judgment day.
In myriad replica we wage; Unmoved, then, Soul, by earth's alarms
Remember happy England: keep
Her peace that long hath lulled to sleep, May now exact the sleep of death.
With harvest now are richly at rest; Safe in her isled securities,
The sun from out her Eastern seas Would bring the dust which in her sight
Come, Death, I'd have a word with thee;
And Love--a lad with broken wing; And Pity, too:
As Fools will sing.
And a tune's soon told, And Earth is old,
Yet have I secrets,--dark, my dear, To breathe you all: Come near.
I'll ring my bells.
Yes, yes, their bodies go 'Neath burning sun and icy star
Dragging cold cannon through a mire Of rain and blood and spouting fire,
Wide with insanities!
I hardly know the meaning of; And the mute birds
From out their shade of leaf and flower, Trembling at treacheries
Heed, heed not what I said Of frenzied hosts of men,
On envy, hatred fed, Who kill, and die--
Yet Pity whispered, 'Why?'
Mine was not news for child to know, And Death--no ears hath. He hath supped where creep
Yet, when he smiles, the hand he draws Athwart his grinning jaws--
Hearken how my bells in the air Drive away care!...
Of a world all mad. Not simple happy mad like me,
Of water and willow tree, Where the wind hath been;
Who rots in his own head, And counts the dead,
But for the ghosts they were, Brave, faithful, true,
In Earth's clear green and blue Heaven they did share
There, now! Death goes--
Ay, and the light doth dim, And asleep's the rose,
In dreams is hence.... Come, Love, my lad,
'Tis time thy prayers were said!
Let the foul Scene proceed:
'Tis sawdust that they bleed, But a box Death brings.
These extreme pangs to show, How real a frenzy wears
Gigantic dins uprise!
A smarting of the eyes As these fumes upsweal.
While we Spectators sit, Aghast at its agony,
Dark is the outer air,
Mutely we stare, and stare At the frenzied Show.
Of deep, immutable blue-- We cry 'An end!' We are bowed
While the Shape who hoofs applause
Hoots--angel-wise--'the Cause!' And affright ev'n fear.
You sleep too well--too far away,
Your very quiet seems to say How longed-for a peace you have found.
You would have grieved--'twixt joy and fear-- To know how my small loving son
Roses are sweet to smell and see,
But rarer, stranger buds there be, And she was like to them.
More lovely shade than light, That, setting, silvers lonely hills
Close to the world of my poor heart
Now that she's gone, O dark, and dark, The solitude--the fear.
Never, no never, listen too long,
bird's song.
'Tis sad in sooth to lie under the grass,
where life's shadows pass.
And, for every green copper battered and worn, doles out Nevers and Nots.
Who with a sharp ear listens and listens the whole world through.
With platter and finger and spoon--and good victuals at least.
Clear eyes do dim at last,
Time, heedless of the past, No loving-kindness knows;
Still Lethe flows.
And sorrow, being o'er, Its salt tears shed away,
Stealthily lave those waters That solemn shore.
While yet quick memory lives! And Sorrow, ere thou art gone,
Ere yet, grown cold in peace, It loves not, nor grieves.
Heavenly Archer, bend thy bow;
Youth is gone; I, too, would go.
Harsh or kind, at last she is Murderess of all ecstasies.
Bound in sense, still hearkens on For tidings of a bliss foregone.
At no breath astonished, From the Gardens of the Dead.
By Babylon's river languishing. Heavenly Archer, loose thy string.
Far are those tranquil hills,
On urgent, secret errand bent, A traveller goes.
Barefooted, cowled; their eyes Scan the lone, hastening solitary
One instant in close speech
God-sped, he hasteneth on, That anxious traveller...
And each world's night in vain I patient wait on sleep to unveil
Would that they three could know
Love--from one lost in Paradise-- For their grave courtesy.
It was the Great Alexander,
Sate in the ages, in his floating ship, In a dead calm.
Wandered across the deep: The sailors labouring on their oars
All the high pomp of Asia,
Out of their weary and dreaming minds, Faded away.
His glamour withered and gone, In the souls of his brooding mariners,
Time, like a falling dew,
Laid between slumber and slumber, Only did seem....
In all us mortals too, Wax thou not bold--too bold
Come the calm, infinite night,
Aught save the singing Of the sea-maids clear?
Green in light are the hills, and a calm wind flowing Filleth the void with a flood of the fragrance of Spring; Wings in this mansion of life are coming and going,
Coloured with buds of delight the boughs are swaying,
Flowers from wintry sleep, her enchantment obeying, Stir in the deep of her dream, reawaken to love.

Oh, now begone sullen care--this light is my seeing; I am the palace, and mine are its windows and walls; Daybreak is come, and life from the darkness of being Springs, like a child from the womb, when the lonely one calls.
As I did walk in meadows green
With call of myriad things unseen That leapt and crept upon the ground.
Throbbed with the homesick coursing cry Of swallows that did everywhere
Beside me, too, clear waters coursed
Breaking their crystal gliding forced To sing as they did flow.
With praise no language could express; Longing in vain for him to come
On this fair world, wherein we pass
And yearned in spirit to learn, alas, What kept him still away.
How do the days press on, and lay
Whileas the stars in darkness play And moonbeams weave a crown--
Where in the hollow arch of space Morn's mistress dreams, and the Pleiads seven
Stand watch--O days no number keep
When the world's clocks are dumb in sleep 'Tis then I seek my kind.
In the strange city of Life
One wherein Silence a garden hath, And one where Dark doth dwell.
Shadowing the dizzied street, Where Vanity flaunts her gilded booths
Green-graped upon their walls
Hath clustered their carven, lichenous stones With tendril serpentine.
Dazed in that clamorous throng, I thirst for the soundless fount that stills
Knock, knock, nor knock in vain:
Where Silence a fast-sealed garden hath, Where Dark doth dwell.
For all the grief I have given with words
In the dust, and the heat, and the silence of birds, Where the lonely go.
Be a dark, cool water calling--calling To the footsore, benighted, solitary,
O, be beauty for all my blindness,
And dews burdened with loving-kindness In the dark of the end.
What lovely things
The smooth-plumed bird In its emerald shade,
The speck of stone Which the wayfaring ant
Though I should sit
Using its ink As the spirit wills
Its live, willed things, Flit would the ages
Ere unto Z My pen drew nigh;
And the honey-fly: And still would remain
My worn reeds broken, The dark tarn dry,
Thou, Lord, and I.
When I lie where shades of darkness
Nor the rain make lamentation When the wind sighs;
Was the very proof of me? Memory fades, must the remembered
Oh, when this my dust surrenders
May these loved and loving faces Please other men!
Still the Traveller's Joy entwine, And as happy children gather
Look thy last on all things lovely,
Seal thy sense in deathly slumber Till to delight
Since that all things thou wouldst praise Beauty took from those who loved them
